item.title: How Does Property Compare with Other Assets in an Uncertain Market?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

During periods of economic volatility, investors and homeowners often reassess their asset allocation strategies. UK residential property has long been considered a relatively stable investment compared to more volatile markets, but how does bricks-and-mortar measure up against alternatives like equities, commodities and fixed-income securities when uncertainty looms?

Property Versus Traditional Asset Classes

Property investment offers several distinctive characteristics during turbulent times. Unlike stocks which can swing dramatically within hours, residential property values tend to move more gradually, providing a cushion against sudden market shocks. The UK's chronic housing shortage also provides fundamental support to prices, though liquidity is considerably lower than with securities.

When comparing property to gold - the classic 'safe haven' asset - the differences are pronounced. Gold provides instant liquidity and acts as a hedge against inflation, but generates no income. Residential property offers rental yields alongside capital growth potential, though requires active management. Bonds typically deliver steadier returns than property but currently struggle to outpace inflation, while equities may offer higher growth potential but with greater volatility.

Key Considerations for Property Investors

For those considering property investment during uncertain periods, several factors warrant careful attention:

  • Location resilience: Certain UK regions and property types have historically shown more stability during downturns
  • Rental demand: Areas with strong employment markets tend to maintain better occupancy rates
  • Financing costs: Mortgage rates significantly impact investment returns, making product selection crucial
  • Tax efficiency: Recent changes to landlord taxation have altered the maths for some investors

Property's tangible nature often appeals to investors wary of more abstract financial instruments during unstable periods. The ability to add value through refurbishment or development can also provide returns not available with purely financial assets.

Whilst past performance never guarantees future results, UK residential property has demonstrated considerable resilience through various economic cycles, though typically with less dramatic highs and lows than more liquid markets. Investors might consider how property could complement other assets in their portfolio rather than viewing it as an either/or proposition.

item.title: House price growth stalls as estate agents warn of further falls
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market has shown signs of stagnation, with annual house price growth remaining at 1.2% as of September 2023, according to the latest data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Average house prices in the UK now stand at £273,000, reflecting a subdued market influenced by higher mortgage costs, reduced buyer confidence, and ongoing affordability challenges. Whilst this figure represents modest growth, the national average conceals significant regional variations, with some areas experiencing sharper declines while others continue to see price increases.

Regional Variations in House Price Trends

The ONS figures highlight stark differences in property price movements across the UK. In England, house prices rose by just 0.8% annually, while Wales and Scotland saw stronger growth at 1.8% and 2.3% respectively. London remains the weakest performer, with prices falling by 3.5% over the year. Inner London recorded an even steeper decline of 7.2%, marking its most significant annual drop since August 2009. In contrast, the North East of England emerged as the strongest regional market, with prices climbing by 4.6% over the same period.

These regional disparities underscore the uneven impact of economic pressures on the property market. Factors such as local affordability, demand, and employment opportunities continue to shape trends, creating a patchwork of growth and decline across the country.

Shifting Dynamics for Buyers and Sellers

Estate agents report that the current market conditions are prompting changes in buyer behaviour. With higher mortgage costs and weaker consumer confidence, buyers are taking longer to make decisions and are increasingly selective about their purchases. This shift has given buyers greater negotiating power, particularly in areas where properties are overpriced or where demand is softer.

Nicky Stevenson, managing director of Fine & Country, emphasised the importance of realistic pricing for sellers. “Buyers now have more choice than they’ve had in years, meaning overpriced properties are increasingly likely to be overlooked. The difference between setting the right asking price from the outset and having to reduce it later can be significant.” Similarly, Verona Frankish, CEO of Yopa, noted that the challenge for sellers lies not just in achieving a strong price but in finding the right buyer in a more cautious market.

Daniel Clarke, founder of Homebuyer.Agency, added that whilst buyers have more room to negotiate, they should not assume they can dictate prices entirely. “A more measured market doesn’t mean buyers can simply name their price. Realistic offers and careful negotiation remain key.”

Rising Rents and Market Outlook

As the property market slows, rental demand continues to grow, pushing UK private rents up by 3.8% in the year to October 2023. The average monthly rent now stands at £1,411, adding further pressure on tenants and highlighting the broader affordability challenges facing the housing market.

Looking ahead, industry experts suggest that house prices could face further downward pressure if mortgage costs remain high and economic uncertainty persists. Whilst the market has shown resilience in some areas, the combination of affordability constraints and cautious buyer behaviour may continue to weigh on growth in the coming months.

For homeowners and prospective buyers, staying informed about local market trends and seeking professional advice could prove invaluable in navigating these challenging conditions.

item.title: Rental demand takes unexpected dip as sales market holds steady
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data from Propertymark has revealed an unexpected dip in tenant registrations across the UK rental market, raising questions about shifting demand dynamics. Whilst the sales market has remained relatively stable, the lettings sector appears to be experiencing a slowdown, even as rental costs continue to rise. This development comes amidst ongoing economic uncertainty, prompting both tenants and landlords to reassess their positions.

Rental Market Faces Unusual Slowdown

According to Propertymark’s latest Housing Insight Report, letting agents reported fewer tenant registrations in September compared to previous months. This decline marks a potential departure from recent trends, though it remains unclear whether this signals a long-term shift in demand. Despite rental inflation easing in recent months, overall monthly costs continue to climb, adding pressure to tenants already grappling with affordability challenges.

Nathan Emerson, Chief Executive of Propertymark, commented on the findings, stating, “Whilst rental inflation has slowed, monthly costs are still rising, underscoring the ongoing pressures faced by tenants.” This suggests that affordability issues may be influencing tenant activity, with many households prioritising essential expenses over moving or securing new rental agreements.

Sales Market Shows Resilience

In contrast to the rental sector, the UK sales market has demonstrated greater stability. Propertymark’s report highlights that transaction volumes have remained steady compared to the previous year, with gross mortgage advances showing little significant movement. This indicates that buyers and sellers are continuing to transact despite higher borrowing costs and broader economic uncertainties.

Emerson noted, “The number of property transactions has remained consistent with last year’s figures, and gross mortgage advances have also stayed relatively stable.” However, mortgage affordability and household finances remain key factors influencing purchasing decisions, with many potential buyers carefully weighing their options before committing to a property purchase.

Landlord Investment Under Pressure

The report also sheds light on the challenges facing landlords and property investors. Economic uncertainty, coupled with rising financing costs, has made portfolio expansion increasingly difficult. Many landlords are reassessing their investments in light of these pressures, with some opting to hold off on further acquisitions or even reduce their existing portfolios.

This cautious approach could have implications for the rental market’s future supply, potentially exacerbating affordability issues for tenants if fewer properties become available. For those considering entering the buy-to-let market, it could be worth carefully evaluating current conditions and seeking professional advice to navigate the complexities of property investment in the current climate.

As the UK property market continues to evolve, homeowners, tenants, and investors alike may wish to stay informed about these trends. Whilst the sales market remains steady, the rental sector’s unexpected dip highlights the importance of monitoring affordability and demand dynamics in the months ahead.

item.title: London rental bills soar by £2,000 a year in hardest-hit boroughs
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Renters in London are facing significant increases in their housing costs, with annual rental bills in some boroughs soaring by over £2,000, according to recent analysis. The capital’s ongoing shortage of rental properties has driven prices upwards, leaving tenants grappling with higher monthly payments. Data from Benham and Reeves, based on Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures, reveals that average monthly rents across London rose by 3.5% in the year to September, increasing from £2,260 to £2,338. This equates to an additional £936 annually for the average London tenant.

Rental Increases Across Boroughs

While the overall rise is substantial, some boroughs have experienced even sharper hikes. Islington saw the largest increase in cash terms, with average monthly rents climbing by £179, adding £2,148 to annual rental costs. Southwark recorded the steepest percentage rise at 7.3%, translating to an extra £171 per month or £2,052 annually. These two boroughs top the list of areas where renters are facing the most significant financial pressures.

Other boroughs also reported notable increases. Hammersmith and Fulham saw annual rents rise by £1,620, followed by Richmond upon Thames (£1,428), Merton (£1,380), and Greenwich (£1,368). Kensington and Chelsea (£1,320), Wandsworth (£1,260), Hackney (£1,200), Brent (£1,140), and Enfield (£1,128) also experienced four-figure annual increases. Only Kingston upon Thames and Westminster bucked the trend, with average rents falling by 0.4%, equivalent to annual reductions of £96 and £144, respectively.

Shrinking Rental Supply

The rising costs coincide with a continued decline in rental availability across London. Zoopla’s September 2023 figures indicate a 6% year-on-year drop in rental stock, with inner London experiencing a sharper 13% reduction. Rightmove’s third-quarter data also highlights the issue, showing a 9% decline in available rental listings across the capital. These figures suggest that tenants face heightened competition for properties, further driving up prices.

Marc von Grundherr, director of Benham and Reeves, attributed the rising rents to the shrinking rental stock. “London rents have continued to climb over the last year, placing further financial pressure on tenants who are already contending with a high cost of living,” he said. He also expressed concerns about the potential for further supply constraints as landlords face increasing pressures, such as regulatory changes and rising mortgage costs.

As the rental market tightens, tenants may wish to explore their options carefully and consider seeking advice to navigate the challenges. With competition for properties likely to remain fierce, understanding market trends and planning ahead could help mitigate the impact of rising costs.

item.title: Alcaidesa: the Costa del Sol’s overlooked golf corner starts to price in
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For years, the western stretch of Spain's Costa del Sol remained largely undiscovered by property investors, overshadowed by more famous coastal destinations. Yet the area surrounding Alcaidesa, just beyond Sotogrande, has quietly emerged as an attractive option for those seeking golf properties and quieter coastal living.

A Hidden Gem for Golf Enthusiasts

Alcaidesa's reputation as a golfer's paradise has deep roots, with two championship courses drawing visitors for decades. The rolling greens of Alcaidesa Links and Alcaidesa Heathland sit against a dramatic backdrop of the Mediterranean and Gibraltar's iconic rock formation. Whilst golf remains central to its appeal, recent infrastructure developments have broadened the area's attractiveness beyond the fairways.

Property seekers might find Alcaidesa offers relative value compared to neighbouring Sotogrande, with similar amenities at potentially more accessible price points. The region benefits from excellent transport links, including Gibraltar International Airport just 25 minutes away, making it surprisingly convenient for international buyers.

Changing Market Dynamics

Recent years have seen significant investment transforming Alcaidesa's property landscape. Multi-million euro developments have brought new residential complexes, upgraded marina facilities and enhanced leisure offerings. This regeneration appears to be shifting perceptions of the area from a purely golf-focused destination to a more comprehensive lifestyle location.

For British buyers considering overseas property, Alcaidesa presents an interesting case. The combination of established golf infrastructure, improving amenities and proximity to Gibraltar (with its British influences and English-speaking services) creates a familiar environment. Those exploring the market might notice gradual price increases as more investors recognise the area's potential.

As with any overseas property purchase, thorough research remains essential. Exchange rate fluctuations, local tax implications and Spanish property laws all warrant careful consideration alongside the potential lifestyle benefits that Alcaidesa increasingly offers to international buyers.

item.title: Leasehold shake-up could leave some homeowners worse off, expert warns
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The government’s proposed leasehold reforms, designed to simplify and reduce costs for homeowners, might have unintended consequences for certain leaseholders. While the new Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill promises significant changes, experts warn that some property owners could face higher expenses when extending their leases.

Potential Winners and Losers in Leasehold Reforms

The legislation introduces several key changes, including:

  • A £250 annual cap on ground rents
  • Removal of marriage value calculations
  • The option for 990-year lease extensions

However, specialists highlight that the devil lies in the detail. Homeowners with fewer than 80 years remaining on their leases may benefit from the abolition of marriage value. Those currently facing high ground rents could also see financial relief. Yet for leaseholders with longer terms remaining, the situation remains uncertain.

Linz Darlington of Homehold explains: "The Bill doesn’t specify the percentage rates that ultimately determine extension costs. These will be set through secondary legislation, leaving open the possibility that some might pay more than under current rules."

Uncertainty For Property Transactions

The lack of clarity around valuation rates creates practical challenges for:

  • Estate agents trying to accurately price properties
  • Mortgage lenders assessing loan viability
  • Buyers and sellers negotiating leasehold transactions

Until the government confirms the precise calculation methods, professionals across the property sector face difficulties advising clients on lease extension costs. This uncertainty could potentially slow down transactions involving leasehold properties in the coming months.

Questions Over Legislative Safeguards

Concerns have been raised about the absence of guaranteed cost reductions within the Bill. Housing minister Matthew Pennycook previously advocated for stronger protections while in opposition, yet these haven’t been included in the current proposals.

Darlington questions the reasoning behind this omission: "With such a substantial parliamentary majority, the government has ample opportunity to incorporate these safeguards if they choose to do so."

As the legislation progresses through Parliament, homeowners may wish to monitor developments closely. Those considering lease extensions might find it worthwhile to seek professional advice to understand how the reforms could affect their individual circumstances.

item.title: Mortgage borrowers face Christmas interest rate hike as Bank of England issues warning
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Mortgage borrowers could face an unwelcome Christmas surprise this year, as the Bank of England warns of a potential interest rate hike in December. With inflation remaining stubbornly high and global tensions escalating, homeowners might need to brace themselves for further increases in borrowing costs. The Bank’s latest remarks come amidst growing economic uncertainty, leaving many to wonder what this could mean for their mortgage payments and the wider housing market.

Inflation Concerns and Economic Pressures

Recent inflation figures reveal that UK consumer prices rose by 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September. This increase, largely driven by rising fuel and energy costs, has pushed inflation significantly above the Bank of England’s 2% target. Governor Andrew Bailey has cautioned that the ongoing conflict in the Middle East could exacerbate inflationary pressures, potentially necessitating higher interest rates to keep the situation under control. Financial markets are now anticipating a 74% chance of a rate rise when the Monetary Policy Committee meets on 17 December, though this could shift in the coming weeks.

The Bank of England predicts inflation could reach around 5% by mid-2027 as higher energy costs ripple through the economy. Adding to the strain, energy consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 26% rise in typical household energy bills from January, pushing annual gas and electricity costs to approximately £2,166. This increase could further tighten household budgets, reducing spending power and making mortgage affordability even more challenging for prospective buyers.

Mortgage Rates Under Pressure

The prospect of another rate hike has raised concerns among borrowers, many of whom are already grappling with higher mortgage costs. Mark Harris, chief executive of mortgage broker SPF Private Clients, noted that borrowers are facing renewed uncertainty. “Another interest rate increase could be on the cards to curb inflation, potentially coming at next month’s Bank of England meeting,” he said. Swap rates, which influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages, have been climbing in recent days, though lenders have shown mixed reactions, with some trimming their rates.

David Hollingworth, associate director at L&C Mortgages, warned that recent reductions in fixed mortgage rates may not last. “While some lenders have cut their fixed rates in recent weeks, these reductions are unlikely to become a long-term trend,” he explained. For borrowers nearing the end of their fixed-rate deals, this could mean facing significantly higher payments when they remortgage.

Impact on the Housing Market

The potential for further rate rises is also casting a shadow over the housing market, which has already shown signs of slowing down. Estate agents fear that increased mortgage costs could deter buyers, prolonging the current market slowdown. With affordability stretched and household budgets under pressure, the property market may face additional challenges in the months ahead.

For homeowners and prospective buyers alike, staying informed and seeking professional advice could be crucial in navigating these uncertain times. Monitoring market trends and exploring mortgage options may help borrowers make informed decisions as they prepare for potential changes in the economic landscape.

item.title: Landlord and letting agent fines in London near £29m as licensing penalties surge
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

London landlords and letting agents are facing significantly steeper penalties for licensing violations, with total fines recorded on the Mayor of London's Rogue Landlord Database now approaching £29m. Recent analysis by compliance specialists Kamma reveals a near-tripling of fines since April 2024, with licensing offences accounting for 59% of all penalties.

Sharp rise in licensing penalties

The latest figures show £28.8m in total fines, up from £10m recorded earlier this year. Licensing-related penalties alone have reached £16.9m, increasing by over £2m since May. The database currently lists 4,592 enforcement actions against 2,113 landlords and agents across the capital.

Recent legislative changes have substantially increased the financial risks for non-compliance. The Renters' Rights Act has raised maximum civil penalties for licensing offences from £30,000 to £40,000, which councils can impose without court proceedings. Meanwhile, tenants in unlicensed properties can now claim up to 24 months' rent through repayment orders - double the previous limit.

Expanding licensing landscape

London's licensing schemes have expanded rapidly, with 29 of the capital's 32 boroughs now operating selective or additional licensing arrangements. Thirteen boroughs have introduced new schemes in the past year alone, including Islington, Enfield and Croydon since August.

This patchwork of local requirements creates particular challenges for agents managing properties across multiple boroughs. Licensing costs, application processes and renewal dates vary significantly between local authorities, meaning identical properties might face completely different compliance obligations just streets apart.

Growing pressure on letting agents

Letting agents account for £11.2m of the recorded fines, with 1,701 enforcement actions taken against companies. The database also shows 352 instances of agents being expelled from property redress schemes for non-compliance.

Orla Shields, CEO of Kamma, commented: "Licensing has transformed from a niche concern to London's primary source of property enforcement action. With maximum penalties now at £40,000 and rent repayment orders doubled, the financial consequences of non-compliance have never been more severe."

Property professionals operating in multiple boroughs may wish to pay particular attention to their compliance systems as the regulatory landscape continues to evolve rapidly across the capital.

item.description:

Recent research from Aldermore Bank highlights a significant shift in the buy-to-let property market, with landlords selling rental properties at four times the rate of new purchases. Landlords rebalancing property portfolios

Market analysts suggest several factors may be influencing this trend, including recent tax changes, stricter regulations, and shifting property values across different regions.

Smaller landlords appear to be leading this exodus, often citing increased administrative burdens and reduced profit margins as key reasons for selling up. Meanwhile, professional investors with larger portfolios are taking advantage of market conditions to acquire additional properties, potentially benefiting from economies of scale that smaller operators cannot match.

Market consolidation creates new opportunities

This divergence between small-scale and large-scale landlords is creating a two-tier market. Property professionals note that experienced investors with substantial portfolios are often better positioned to navigate the current regulatory environment and absorb higher operating costs.

  • Regional variations in property prices and rental yields may favour certain locations
  • Mortgage products tailored for portfolio landlords could offer competitive terms
  • Tax planning strategies may help mitigate some of the recent fiscal changes

item.title: Rent arrears biggest cause of repossessions
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent research from the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has highlighted that unpaid rent remains the primary reason landlords seek possession of rental properties. This comes amidst growing concerns over escalating taxes and housing costs, which are putting additional pressure on both tenants and landlords.

The Impact of Rent Arrears

Rent arrears have emerged as a significant issue in the UK rental market, with many landlords facing financial strain due to unpaid rent. According to the NRLA, this is the leading cause of repossessions, as landlords struggle to cover their own costs, including mortgage payments, maintenance, and rising taxes. For tenants, falling behind on rent can lead to eviction proceedings, creating a cycle of financial instability.

Challenges for Landlords

Landlords are finding it increasingly difficult to navigate the financial pressures of the current housing market. Rising taxes, including changes to mortgage interest relief and stamp duty, have added to their financial burdens. Additionally, the cost of maintaining properties and complying with regulatory requirements has increased. These factors, combined with rent arrears, have forced many landlords to consider repossession as a last resort.

  • Financial Strain: Landlords face mounting costs, including mortgage payments and property maintenance.
  • Regulatory Pressures: Compliance with new regulations adds to the financial burden.
  • Tax Changes: Recent tax reforms have reduced profitability for many landlords.

Support for Tenants and Landlords

To address these challenges, both tenants and landlords may benefit from exploring available support options. Tenants struggling to pay rent could seek advice from housing charities or local councils, whilst landlords might consider engaging with tenants early to discuss payment plans or seek mediation services. Government initiatives and support schemes could also play a role in alleviating financial pressures on both parties.

As the rental market continues to evolve, it is essential for both tenants and landlords to stay informed about their rights and responsibilities. By addressing rent arrears proactively and seeking support where needed, it may be possible to reduce the number of repossessions and create a more stable rental environment for all involved.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH! Government unveils sweeping leasehold reforms as campaigners celebrate and industry backlash erupts
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has announced radical reforms to England and Wales' centuries-old leasehold system, marking what ministers describe as the most significant transformation of property ownership in generations. The proposed legislation aims to empower millions of leaseholders while sparking debate across the housing sector.

Key Changes in the Leasehold Reform Bill

The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill introduces several fundamental changes to property ownership structures. From 2028, ground rents will be capped at £250 annually before gradually reducing to zero over 40 years. The controversial 'marriage value' calculation used in lease extensions will be abolished, potentially making freehold purchases more affordable for existing leaseholders.

Other notable measures include:

  • Stronger protections against excessive administration and permission charges
  • Replacement of forfeiture powers with court-led processes for unpaid charges
  • New powers to cap fees for property alterations or pet ownership
  • Commonhold becoming the default ownership model for new flats

The government estimates these reforms could benefit up to five million leasehold homeowners, with particular focus on addressing what ministers describe as "excessive extraction" from property owners.

Industry Reaction and Potential Impacts

While leasehold campaigners have welcomed the proposals as a long-awaited victory, the reforms have drawn criticism from some property investors and freeholders. Concerns have been raised about the potential impact on existing contracts and pension investments tied to ground rent income streams.

The legislation also extends protections to approximately 1.75 million freehold homeowners on so-called 'fleecehold' estates, where residents pay mandatory maintenance charges. These homeowners will gain new safeguards against aggressive enforcement practices.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook stated: "The leasehold system denies individuals control over the homes they live in, and have paid for. Our reforms mark the beginning of the end for this feudal system." However, some industry voices warn the changes could create uncertainty in parts of the housing market during the transition period.

As the bill enters Parliament, homeowners may wish to monitor its progress and consider seeking professional advice about how the reforms could affect their property rights and financial commitments. The full impact of these changes will become clearer as the legislation moves through the parliamentary process.

item.title: Santander joins six-times-income mortgage race as buyers offered bigger loans
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Santander has joined the growing number of lenders offering mortgages of up to six times annual income, potentially boosting borrowing power for eligible first-time buyers by up to £90,000. The bank has increased its maximum loan-to-income (LTI) multiple from five to six times earnings for qualifying applicants, provided they meet specific criteria. This move could help buyers struggling to bridge the gap between rising property prices and their incomes, though experts caution that larger loans may lead to higher repayments and could impact housing affordability in certain areas.

What has changed with Santander’s mortgage criteria?

Under the new rules, first-time buyers with a minimum household income of £45,000 and a deposit of at least 10% may now be eligible for mortgages of up to six times their income. For example, a buyer earning £60,000 could potentially borrow £360,000, up from £300,000 under the previous five-times-income limit. Similarly, a household earning £90,000 could see their maximum borrowing increase from £450,000 to £540,000.

The higher multiple also extends to home movers and remortgage customers with individual or joint incomes of at least £100,000. For instance, a household earning £100,000 could now borrow up to £600,000, compared to £550,000 previously. However, all applications remain subject to Santander’s affordability assessments and wider lending criteria.

How does Santander compare to other lenders?

Santander’s decision brings it in line with several major competitors, including Nationwide, Barclays, NatWest, and HSBC, which already offer mortgages of up to six times income under varying eligibility requirements. Aaron Strutt of Trinity Financial noted that Santander risked losing business to rivals offering higher borrowing multiples. He commented: “The lender was already generous, offering up to 5.5 times salary, but not as competitive as some of its peers. This change will likely be welcomed by customers.”

item.title: Charlie Lamdin hits back at estate agents: ‘You’re missing the point’
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The founder of BestAgent, Charlie Lamdin, has responded to criticism from estate agents regarding the platform’s use of property listings, marketing materials, and viewing arrangements. Lamdin emphasised that basic property information will remain on BestAgent, even if agents request the removal of additional content such as photographs and floorplans. His comments come amidst ongoing debates about who controls property marketing material once it is published online.

Debate Over Property Listings

The dispute arose after concerns were raised by Andrew Muskett, manager at David Burr’s Woolpit office in Suffolk, regarding BestAgent’s use of his agency’s marketing material and handling of viewing enquiries. The discussion gained traction following an article in EYE, which sparked further debate among estate agents. Some commentators drew parallels with Houser, a property website that previously faced controversy for its approach to reproducing agents’ listings.

Lamdin defended BestAgent’s practices, stating that basic property information, such as the address, price, size, energy rating, and sold history, is publicly available and not subject to copyright. He argued that agents demanding the removal of listings are “missing the point” and highlighted that fewer than 1% of agents listed on the platform have raised complaints.

Who Controls Marketing Material?

The controversy has reignited questions about the control of property marketing material once it is published online. Lamdin stressed that while agents can request the removal of photographs, floorplans, and descriptions, the underlying property information will remain visible on BestAgent. He also urged agents to consider the implications of removing marketing content, particularly in relation to their obligations to vendors.

Lamdin stated, “Every seller pays their agent to market their home well. An agent who pulls the marketing will need to consider whether that’s in their seller’s best interests, and be ready to explain that choice to their seller.” This statement underscores the potential conflict between agents’ desire to control their marketing material and their duty to act in the best interests of their clients.

The ongoing debate highlights the evolving relationship between estate agents and third-party platforms in the digital age. As the property market continues to adapt to new technologies, the question of who controls online property information remains a contentious issue.

item.title: Misleading property advert lands OnTheMarket and estate agent in trouble with ASA
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has ruled against property portal OnTheMarket and estate agency Edward Mellor following complaints about a misleading shared ownership property advert. The case highlights the importance of clear pricing information when marketing part-buy, part-rent homes.

Shared ownership details omitted from advert

The disputed listing promoted a two-bedroom semi-detached bungalow with the headline "From £107,500". However, this figure represented only a 50% share of the property, with potential buyers also facing ongoing rent payments, service charges and insurance costs. The advert failed to mention these additional financial commitments or the development's age restrictions requiring residents to be at least 55 years old and retired.

OnTheMarket argued that their display advert simply directed users to a full listing containing all necessary details. The ASA rejected this defence, stating that consumers might reasonably assume the advertised price reflected full ownership. The regulator emphasised that shared ownership arrangements fundamentally change the nature of a property purchase and this information should appear in initial marketing materials.

Incorrect monthly cost information provided

The investigation also revealed discrepancies in the advertised monthly outgoings. Edward Mellor initially listed the rent as £325 per month based on information from the seller and housing association. The agency later received updated figures showing the total monthly charges actually amounted to £375.30, comprising:

  • £249.09 rent
  • £112.52 service charge
  • £13.70 insurance

While the estate agent updated their marketing upon receiving the correct details, the ASA ruled they should have disclosed the service charge amount from the outset. The watchdog found the advert breached advertising codes by omitting material information that could influence a consumer's decision to enquire about the property.

This ruling serves as a reminder to both estate agents and property portals about their responsibilities when advertising shared ownership homes. Potential buyers might wish to check whether properties are being sold under shared ownership schemes when they see prices that appear particularly low for an area.

item.title: Buy-to-let landlords abandon plans to sell as falling flat prices derail exit strategies
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent research suggests a notable shift in buy-to-let landlord strategies, with many reconsidering property sales as flat price declines alter their financial calculations. According to estate agency Winkworth's Autumn Prime Outer London Report, fluctuating valuations and changing market conditions have led some landlords to remain in the rental sector rather than exiting as previously planned.

Market fluctuations prompt landlord rethink

Winkworth's data reveals a striking reversal in landlord behaviour between summer and autumn 2023. During the summer months, when the Renters' Rights Act came into force, sales valuations jumped by 18% while lettings valuations dropped by 21%. However, as autumn approached and flat prices softened, some landlords opted to keep properties in the rental market, leading to a 15% annual increase in new lettings instructions across several prime London areas including Clapham, Fulham and St John's Wood.

Mohammad Copley, insights manager at Winkworth, noted: "Our offices' dual focus on sales and lettings provides real-time visibility of landlord decision-making. The changing market dynamics have clearly influenced many investors' strategies."

Regional variations and market impacts

The research uncovered significant regional differences in landlord behaviour. In Clapham and St John's Wood, disappointing sales valuations and strong rental yields have encouraged landlords to retain properties. Meanwhile, areas like Fulham and Parsons Green have seen smaller portfolio owners increasingly opting to sell, often citing growing costs and administrative pressures.

The return of some landlords to the rental market has eased competition among tenants. Whereas summer saw nearly 23 registered tenants competing for each available property, this ratio dropped to around 16 by autumn as supply improved. The report also highlighted a growing divergence between property types, with family homes priced above £1.5 million continuing to attract buyers in several locations, while flats face challenges including higher service charges and building safety concerns.

With further tax changes on the horizon - including increased rental income tax rates from April 2027 - many buy-to-let investors may find themselves regularly reassessing their strategies in response to both market conditions and regulatory shifts.

item.title: Santander joins battle to fix broken property sales process
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research reveals that UK property transactions now take an average of 120 days to reach exchange – a 54% increase compared to 2016 figures. With one in four sales collapsing before completion, Santander has joined industry efforts to streamline the process through the National Property Transaction Network (NPTN).

Growing delays in property transactions

Data from Connells Group shows the average time between sale agreement and exchange has extended from 78 days in 2016 to 120 days in 2026. Even market leaders like Connells, whose transactions complete in 110 days on average, face significantly longer timelines than a decade ago. These delays create uncertainty for all parties and increase the risk of transactions falling through.

Chris Rosindale, Chief Operating Officer at Connells Group, commented: "Whilst our performance remains stronger than the market average, today's 110-day timeline still represents an extra month of uncertainty compared to 2016. This clearly demonstrates the need for systemic improvements."

The high cost of failed transactions

Santander's research highlights the financial impact of prolonged sales processes, with their Fixing the Broken Chain report estimating that:

  • 25% of property transactions fail before completion
  • Failed sales cost affected parties an average of £1,240
  • The annual economic impact exceeds £1.5 billion

Lengthy transaction processes account for 19% of collapsed sales, while survey issues contribute to 16% of failures. When deals collapse late in the process – as happens with one in five failed transactions – buyers, sellers and agents face particularly significant setbacks.

Industry collaboration for faster completions

Santander has joined Lloyds Banking Group, Skipton Building Society, Connells Group and technology provider LMS in supporting the NPTN initiative. This collaboration aims to modernise the property transaction process through:

  • Improved communication between parties
  • Standardised documentation
  • Technology-driven solutions

For homeowners considering a move, these industry developments could eventually lead to more reliable transaction timelines. In the current market, allowing additional time for completion and preparing for potential delays might help reduce stress during the moving process.
